meta.framework: Corporations Act 2001 (Cth), Chapter 7 (Pt 7.7 Financial Services Disclosure; Pt 7.9 Financial Product Disclosure), and Corporations Regulations 2001
meta.legislative_currency_note: Provisions verified against AustLII / ASIC sources as at 2026-08. The SOA regime (s946A) is current but has a proposed successor: under DBFO Tranche 2 the SOA is slated to be replaced by a Client Advice Record (CAR). Tranche 2 was not yet passed as at this build. See 'reform_watch'. Do not hardcode 'SOA' as the only advice-record type — classify by role in the advice process, carry the statutory label as an attribute.
meta.not_legal_advice: This maps documents to provisions to drive classification. It is not legal advice and does not substitute for a financial-services lawyer's sign-off, especially on the AFSL boundary and on reform timing.
meta.consumers: Each document entry feeds: (1) new-to-industry teaching layer, (2) classifier identification hints, (3) version-tracking logic. Single source of truth — do not fork copies into the UI or classifier.

dbfo_tranche_2.status: Draft legislation released 21 March 2025; delayed through 2025-2026; not passed as at this build.
dbfo_tranche_2.impact: SOA to be replaced by 'Client Advice Record' (CAR) — intended to be shorter, principles-based. Proposed CAR content: the words 'client advice record'; scope of advice; the advice; reasons (how it meets client objectives/situation/needs); cost of advice and benefits to provider; providing entity name/contact and authorised-representative status.
dbfo_tranche_2.also_proposed: Removal/streamlining of the s961B(2) safe-harbour steps; shift from prescriptive process to outcomes.
dbfo_tranche_2.design_implication: DECIDED 2026-09-05: 'car' is NOT carried as a document type while it is unlegislated — the system does not classify or file document types that are not law. The transition seam is advice_record_role, which is still carried by 'soa' and 'roa', so role-keyed logic stays exercised. Because the supported type set is read from this file rather than hardcoded, adding the successor type on enactment is a data change: one entry here, no Python. That property is asserted by a test rather than assumed — see tests/test_scope_gate.py, test_a_new_advice_record_type_needs_no_code_change.

advice_types.name: Personal advice
advice_types.plain: Advice given where the provider has considered one or more of the client's objectives, financial situation or needs (or a reasonable person would expect them to have). Triggers the SOA/ROA regime and the best-interests duty (s961B).

advice_types.name: General advice
advice_types.plain: Financial product advice that is not personal advice. No SOA; instead a general-advice warning is required.
not_yet_document_types: general advice warning — usually a paragraph inside another document rather than a file of its own; not modelled as a type (see #23)

advice_types.name: Scaled (limited-scope) personal advice
advice_types.provision: Personal advice; scope limited by agreement. RG 244.
advice_types.plain: Personal advice limited in subject matter (e.g. one topic). Still personal advice — SOA/ROA and best-interests duty apply, assessed against the agreed scope.

advice_types.name: Further advice
advice_types.provision: notional s946B(2)-(3), as substituted by reg 7.7.10AE
advice_types.plain: Subsequent personal advice to a client with an existing SOA, where their circumstances and the basis of advice are not significantly different. May be recorded via ROA instead of a fresh SOA.
advice_types.same_as: documents[roa].legislation.situations[further_advice]. This entry is the TYPE of advice; that one is the ROA SITUATION it permits. Same id on purpose — they are the same thing seen from two sides. The other two ROA situations (no_buy_sell, small_investment) have no advice_types entry because they describe when an ROA is allowed, not a kind of advice.

advice_types.name: Execution-only / no advice
advice_types.provision: No personal advice given (s766B not engaged)
advice_types.plain: Client instructs a transaction with no personal recommendation. No SOA/ROA; dealing and product-disclosure rules still apply.

advice_process_stages.name: Engagement & disclosure
advice_process_stages.plain: The relationship is established; the client is told who the provider is, what they offer, and how they're paid — before any service is provided.

advice_process_stages.name: Discovery / fact-find
advice_process_stages.plain: The provider gathers the client's goals, financial situation, and risk tolerance — the evidentiary basis for the best-interests duty.

advice_process_stages.name: Advice construction
advice_process_stages.plain: Recommendations are formed and the reasoning/basis for advice is documented.

advice_process_stages.name: Advice delivery
advice_process_stages.plain: The advice record is given to the client, at or as soon as practicable after the advice.
governing_provisions: s946B (ROA path: reg 7.7.10AE further advice; reg 7.7.10AAA no buy or sell; s946AA small investment)

advice_process_stages.name: Implementation / execution
advice_process_stages.plain: The client authorises action and the recommendations are executed; product applications are lodged.
governing_provisions: General s912A conduct; product application terms; dealing provisions
not_yet_document_types: product application forms — not yet a document type (see #23)

advice_process_stages.name: Ongoing service & review
advice_process_stages.plain: Periodic review; ongoing fee arrangements are disclosed and consented to; smaller changes may be recorded rather than fully re-advised.
governing_provisions: Ongoing fee arrangement / consent provisions (Div 3 Pt 7.7A, as amended by DBFO Tranche 1)

version_status_values.current: The live, in-force version of this document for this client (or this edition, for licensee/issuer-wide docs).
version_status_values.draft: Work in progress, not yet issued.
version_status_values.superseded: Was current; replaced by a newer version of the same document type and scope.
version_status_values.duplicate: Content match of a document already on file — no new information.
version_status_values.unknown: Could not be confidently placed. Routed to the internal flagging queue for human review.

documents.name: Statement of Advice

legislation.primary: s946A — obligation to give an SOA when personal advice is provided to a retail client
related: s946B — situations where an SOA is not required
s947D — additional content where advice recommends product replacement/switching
s961B/s961G — best interests & appropriate advice underpinning the content
legislation.penalty_note: s946A obligations sit within the civil-penalty framework (s1317E); content failures also expose the licensee via s912A.

teaching.what_it_is: The formal written record of personal financial advice given to a retail client, together with the reasons for it.
teaching.why_it_exists: Required by s946A so the client can understand and decide whether to rely on the advice. It makes the basis of advice, risks, costs, and remuneration explicit and reviewable.
teaching.where_it_sits: Advice construction and delivery (stages 3-4). The centrepiece deliverable of the advice process.
teaching.two_weeks_in_note: If you learn to recognise one document, make it this. Everything else is input to it, disclosure around it, a lighter follow-up to it (ROA), or its implementation (ATP). Note the coming CAR reform — same role, new label.

distinguishing_signals: s947D switching disclosure when products are being replaced
an Authority to Proceed is frequently appended at the end
confusable_with: roa — a full SOA stands alone; an ROA references a prior SOA and is shorter

a document titled 'Client Advice Record' — the proposed DBFO Tranche 2 successor, NOT legislated and deliberately not a document type here (see reform_watch). It has no type to match, so it routes to review rather than being filed as advice whose legal status we cannot determine.
fsg — the FSG is about the provider, not client-specific recommendations

links_to.note: The ATP authorises the client to proceed with THIS SOA's recommendations. Often physically appended to the SOA PDF — a frequent multi-document-bundle split point.
Later further advice on the same basis may be recorded as an ROA referencing this SOA.
The SOA's recommendations must trace back to the fact find and risk profile.

documents.version_notes: Client-specific and dated. A new SOA for the same client and scope supersedes the prior one; rarely a true duplicate.

documents.name: Record of Advice

legislation.primary: s946B — situations in which an SOA is not required (the ROA pathway)
legislation.situation_count_note: THREE situations, not four. ASIC's own FAQ (Table 1) lists three, and s946B(7) is not a separate 'hold / no action' basis: the Act's s946B(7) is the no-buy/sell provision, and reg 7.7.10AAA is the regulation that substitutes a notional version of it and sets its content requirements — its title is literally 'Record of advice without a recommendation to purchase or sell'. Carrying them as two bases counted one situation twice. Advice to HOLD is not a basis at all: it is what the advice recommends, and it sits under further advice where there is a prior SOA, or under no buy or sell where there is not. Decided 17 Sep 2026; see issue #33.
legislation.unresolved: ASIC's 2021 media release describes INFO 266 as explaining 'four exemptions from providing a statement of advice'. Only three ROA situations have been found. The fourth may be a different exemption entirely rather than a fourth ROA basis. Recorded so nobody re-derives the question from scratch; it does not change the three below.
legislation.evidence_note: ONLY THE FURTHER-ADVICE SITUATION HAS BEEN MATCHED AGAINST REAL TEXT. Each situation carries an `example_status` saying whether a real document of that kind exists to test against. Two of the three have none, so their signals are a reading of the legislation rather than anything measured, and should be treated as a starting point to correct against real firm files — not as calibrated. Stated here rather than left to be inferred from silence, because a signal list looks equally authoritative whether or not anything checked it.
legislation.signal_note: Each situation carries `basis_signals`, split into `declared` and `inferred`. DECLARED phrases are the document stating its own basis — naming the situation or citing the provision. INFERRED phrases describe the shape of the recommendation, which suggests a basis without asserting one. Where any situation is declared, only declared signals decide: a document that says which situation it was written under outranks a basis guessed from how the advice reads. Inferred signals decide only when nothing is declared anywhere. Signals are deliberately narrow, because a signal that fires wrongly produces a confident wrong proposal while one that fails to fire produces "which kind is this?" — the honest answer, and this flag's default.
legislation.calibration_note: Measured against ASIC INFO 266 attachment 1 (further advice; retain existing products and increase insurance cover). Two lessons, both from real text. First, "you will retain your existing policy features and benefits" describes a CONSEQUENCE of advice, not a recommendation to hold — so retain/continue-to-hold phrasing was removed entirely. Second, that ROA's own words include "My advice is to make no changes to your XYZ Superannuation Fund" while it also increases insurance cover. Under the three-situation model that document is further advice whose RECOMMENDATION is partly no-change, which is exactly the distinction the old four-basis list could not express.

situations.basis: notional s946B(2)-(3), as substituted by reg 7.7.10AE
situations.when: The client has a previous SOA (or pre-licensing advice), their relevant circumstances are not significantly different from when that advice was given, and the basis of the further advice is not significantly different either.
situations.example_status: Real text available, and it is the only situation with any. All three ASIC INFO 266 example ROAs cite notional s946B(2) and reg 7.7.10AE — including attachment 2, titled 'No change advice', which relies on this situation because the client had an SOA from 2018.

declared: basis of advice has not changed

situations.kind: No buy or sell product advice
situations.basis: notional s946B(7)-(8), as substituted by reg 7.7.10AAA
situations.when: The advice does not recommend or state an opinion on acquiring or disposing of a specific financial product, and does not recommend modifying an investment strategy or a contribution level for a product the client holds.
situations.further_conditions: AND the provider and certain associates receive no remuneration or benefit in relation to the advice, and conflicts are disclosed to the client. This limb is easy to miss and it is decisive: for a client on an ongoing fee arrangement it will usually fail, which is why an annual-review 'no change' recommendation is normally documented as FURTHER advice rather than under this situation. Content alone never establishes this basis.
situations.absorbed: This entry previously appeared twice — as 'hold / no-action (s946B(7))' and as 'no buy/sell (reg 7.7.10AAA)'. They are one situation. See situation_count_note and issue #33.
situations.example_status: NO REAL EXAMPLE. Written from the legislation only. ASIC published no example of this situation. Recorded as a known gap on issues #33 and #35, with the decision not to source one artificially.

declared: no recommendation to acquire or dispose
no recommendation to buy or sell
not a recommendation to acquire or dispose
inferred: does not recommend that you acquire
does not recommend that you dispose

situations.when: Advice relating to financial investments in certain products not exceeding $15,000. Timing rules in reg 7.7.09A(10)-(12).
situations.example_status: NO REAL EXAMPLE. INFO 266 attachment 3 was assumed to be this one from its 'Stockbroker' title; its text contains neither 's946AA' nor 'small investment', and it cites reg 7.7.10AE. See issue #33.

legislation.retention: 7 years after the day the further advice is provided (reg 7.7.09(3); reg 7.7.05; reg 7.7.08)
legislation.content_note: Content requirements differ by kind — chiefly reg 7.7.10AE (further advice) and reg 7.7.10AAA (no buy/sell).

teaching.what_it_is: A shorter record of personal advice used in place of a full SOA in specific situations the Act allows.
teaching.why_it_exists: Reduces paperwork for routine or narrow advice while keeping a durable record. There are three situations in which it is allowed, and which one applies changes what the record must contain. Note that what the advice RECOMMENDS — increase cover, switch, no change — is a separate thing from which situation permits the ROA. Conflating the two is the mistake issue #33 was about.
teaching.two_weeks_in_note: The most common kind (further advice) points back to an earlier SOA. An ROA with no prior SOA on file isn't automatically wrong — the no-buy/sell and small-investment situations don't need one — but it's worth flagging to confirm which kind it is.

key_fields: reference to prior SOA (for further-advice kind)
the recommendation — a change, or no change (what it recommends is separate from which situation permits the ROA)
basis on which recommendations are made
distinguishing_signals: further-advice kind references a prior SOA by date
confusable_with: soa — shorter and (for the further-advice kind) dependent on a prior SOA
file_note — an ROA is client advice; a file note is internal only

links_to.note: The further-advice ROA depends on an existing SOA; the other two situations do not.
Where the ROA advises an action the client then authorises.

documents.version_notes: Sequenced after any SOA. Multiple ROAs coexist as current if they cover different advice events; only same-scope re-issues supersede. Capture WHICH of the three situations — it changes both content expectations and whether a prior SOA is required.

documents.name: Authority to Proceed

legislation.primary: No single dedicated section — it evidences client consent to implement, supporting the licensee's s912A 'efficient, honest and fair' obligation and creating an audit trail for the dealing.
related: Dealing provisions where the implementation involves arranging to acquire a product
legislation.note: Because it isn't a named statutory disclosure document, classification leans on structure (signature/authorisation) and its link to the advice record, not a titling provision.

teaching.what_it_is: The client's signed instruction authorising the adviser to implement the recommendations in an SOA (or ROA).
teaching.why_it_exists: Evidences informed client consent before anything is executed — protecting both parties and showing the client chose to proceed.
teaching.two_weeks_in_note: Very often appended to the back of the SOA it implements. When splitting a scanned bundle, the ATP is the classic 'document 2' hiding at the end of an SOA PDF. Always link it to the advice record it authorises — an ATP with no matching SOA/ROA is an exception worth flagging.

key_fields: the party being authorised — adviser name, authorised-representative number, licensee
reference to the SOA/ROA being authorised
distinguishing_signals: a first-person grant of authority — 'I/We authorise ...' — not a description of advice
names the party receiving the authority, and enumerates the specific actions it covers
prominent signature block binding the client to that grant
references the advice record it implements
may share a document with the SOA
confusable_with: soa — the ATP authorises; the SOA advises

application_forms — both carry a signature and a list of actions, but the authority runs to different parties: an ATP authorises the ADVISER to act, application forms instruct the PRODUCT ISSUER. Read who is being empowered, not what is being signed.
fee_disclosure_statement — also a signed authorisation, but of ongoing FEES rather than of implementing advice

links_to.note: Primary link. Match ATP to its SOA by client + date + referenced recommendations.
Where the action advised in an ROA is the thing being authorised.

documents.version_notes: Per client, per advice event, dated. Not usually superseded — each authorisation is a discrete event. A re-signed ATP for the same advice replaces the earlier one. Firms name this document inconsistently (see title_patterns), so title alone is weak evidence. The substance is constant: can this named party act on the client's behalf, for these specific actions, and did the client grant that authority. Classify on that.

documents.name: Financial Services Guide

legislation.primary: s941A/s941B — obligation to give an FSG; s941D — timing
legislation.timing_rule: Must be given before/at the point a financial service is provided; you cannot provide the service until the FSG is given (s941A, s941B, s941D).

teaching.what_it_is: A disclosure document identifying the provider — who they are, services offered, how they're paid, and how to complain (AFCA).
teaching.why_it_exists: Required by s941A/B so the client can judge who they're dealing with before any service. It's about the provider, not the client.
teaching.where_it_sits: Engagement (stage 1) — usually the first document a client receives.
teaching.two_weeks_in_note: Generic to the licensee/adviser, not tailored to the client — the same FSG goes to many clients. So version tracking here is about which EDITION was in force on a date, not per-client history.

confusable_with: soa — provider-focused and generic vs client-specific advice
pds — a PDS describes a product; the FSG describes the advice service

documents.version_notes: Editioned by effective date, not per client. Track which edition was current on a given date; a newer edition supersedes the prior edition licensee-wide.

documents.name: Product Disclosure Statement

legislation.primary: Part 7.9 — Financial Product Disclosure; a retail client must receive a PDS before acquiring a financial product
legislation.note: Prepared by the product issuer, not the adviser.

teaching.what_it_is: An issuer-prepared document describing a financial product — features, risks, costs, benefits.
teaching.why_it_exists: Required under Pt 7.9 so a client can make an informed decision about a specific product before acquiring it.
teaching.where_it_sits: Referenced during advice construction and implementation (stages 3-5) as supporting information for a recommended product.
teaching.two_weeks_in_note: Issuer-produced and product-specific. Several PDSs in a client file usually means those products were considered or recommended — they're inputs, not the advice itself.

distinguishing_signals: issued by a product provider, not the advice firm
confusable_with: fsg — product vs advice-service
soa — generic issuer material vs personal advice

documents.version_notes: Editioned by issuer and effective date, not per client. A newer PDS edition supersedes the prior edition for that product.

documents.name: Fact Find / Client Data Form

legislation.primary: Not a standalone statutory document, but the evidentiary basis for the best-interests duty (s961B) and appropriate advice (s961G)
related: s912G record-keeping for personal advice (via ASIC Instrument 2024/508)
legislation.note: Its adequacy is judged through the best-interests lens, not a titling provision.

teaching.what_it_is: The structured capture of a client's circumstances — assets, liabilities, income, goals, dependants.
teaching.why_it_exists: Underpins the best-interests duty: without it, advice can't be shown to fit the client.
teaching.two_weeks_in_note: The raw material the SOA is built from. A fact find dated AFTER the SOA it supposedly underpins is a red flag worth surfacing.

confusable_with: risk_profile — narrower, risk-specific
soa — gathers vs advises

links_to.note: The SOA must trace to the fact find; a later-dated fact find is an exception.

documents.version_notes: Per client, dated. A newer fact find supersedes the prior, but retain the prior as history.

documents.name: Risk Profile Questionnaire

legislation.primary: Not standalone; evidences suitability under the best-interests duty (s961B)
legislation.note: Supports matching recommendations to demonstrated risk tolerance.

teaching.what_it_is: A questionnaire and resulting classification of the client's investment risk tolerance.
teaching.why_it_exists: Evidences that recommended investments match the client's risk tolerance, supporting best interests.
teaching.two_weeks_in_note: The risk category should be echoed in the SOA's recommendations. A mismatch between the two is exactly what a reviewer looks for.

distinguishing_signals: narrower than a full fact find
confusable_with: fact_find — narrower, risk-specific
soa — produces a profile not recommendations

links_to.note: Risk category should be consistent with SOA recommendations; inconsistency is a flag.

documents.version_notes: Per client, dated. A re-assessment supersedes the prior profile.

documents.name: File Note

legislation.primary: Not a standalone statutory document. Evidences the research and strategy work behind personal advice — safe harbour steps 3-6 (s961B(2)(c)-(f)) — and is kept under the s912G record-keeping obligation.
legislation.note: No section prescribes its form or title, which is why the titles vary by firm. Its absence is not itself a breach; what it evidences is.

teaching.what_it_is: An adviser's own record of an interaction or of the research behind a recommendation. Often the interaction is with the PRODUCT PROVIDER rather than the client — calling a fund about a balance, a rollover or a policy — as well as client meetings and calls.
teaching.why_it_exists: Safe harbour steps 3-6 (assess competence, investigate, base the advice on that investigation, prioritise the client) happen before the advice record is written and leave no other paper trail. The file note is that trail.
teaching.where_it_sits: Advice construction (stage 3). Sits between discovery and the advice record.
teaching.two_weeks_in_note: A file note is ABOUT advice; it is never the advice. It routinely names a provider and the documents it concerns, which is exactly why it gets mistaken for them. 'File Note - <fund>' records a conversation WITH that fund; it is not that fund's document.

key_fields: the product provider or company contacted
who was spoken to, and in what capacity
distinguishing_signals: written in the adviser's voice, recording what happened, not addressed to the client
past tense narrative of a meeting, a call to a provider, or a piece of research
frequently records a conversation with a PRODUCT PROVIDER, not the client — so a fund's name in it is who was contacted, not who issued it
no recommendation given TO the client, and no signature block
often names the documents it is about — 'an SOA will be prepared', 'the PDS was provided'
title commonly carries the subject after a dash or 'on' — 'File Note - <provider>', 'File Note on <topic>' — so what follows is the subject, not the document type
confusable_with: soa — a file note DESCRIBES advice being prepared; the SOA IS the advice. Not an advice record: advice_record_role is false
roa — both are short and narrative, but an ROA is given to the client as the advice record; a file note stays on the firm's file
pds — a file note naming a product's PDS is a cross-reference, not the PDS. Rank on where the match falls, not that it appears
application_forms — both may carry a provider's name, but an application form INSTRUCTS the provider; a file note merely records talking to them
authority_to_proceed — an ATP is signed by the client and authorises action; a file note is unsigned and authorises nothing

links_to.note: Evidences the research and reasoning behind the advice record it precedes.
Records inquiries made where the fact find was incomplete (safe harbour step 2).

documents.version_notes: Per interaction, not per client or per event. A client accumulates many; they are discrete records, never superseded — a later note does not replace an earlier one.

documents.name: Fee Disclosure Statement / Ongoing Fee Consent

legislation.primary: Ongoing fee arrangement provisions, Div 3 of Pt 7.7A, as amended by DBFO Tranche 1 (single consent regime commenced under DBFO)
legislation.note: DBFO Tranche 1 changed the ongoing-fee/consent mechanics; confirm the current consolidated form on enactment dates.

teaching.what_it_is: Documents disclosing ongoing advice fees and obtaining the client's consent to continue charging them.
teaching.why_it_exists: Protects clients in ongoing fee arrangements by requiring periodic disclosure and renewed consent.
teaching.two_weeks_in_note: This is the area DBFO Tranche 1 already reshaped, so older files and newer files may look different. Flag rather than guess when the format doesn't match the expected era.

key_fields: services the client was entitled to / received
distinguishing_signals: consent/authorisation to continue or deduct fees
confusable_with: authority_to_proceed — ATP authorises implementation of advice; this authorises ongoing FEES
soa — this is fee administration, not advice

documents.version_notes: Per client, periodic (usually annual). Each period's statement is discrete; a corrected re-issue for the same period supersedes.

filing_model.purpose: Defines how classified documents are arranged into folders. Filing is an arrangement of classifier output, not a separate engine. Two nested axes cross-check each other, which improves placement accuracy.

outer.rationale: Matches how firms and compliance reviewers pull files. Stable top level.

inner.rationale: Groups every document belonging to one advisory decision, using the document-to-document links. Reconstructs 'the advice and everything behind it'.

advice_event.definition: A single advisory decision and all documents that belong to it: the advice record (SOA or ROA), the inputs that fed it (fact find, risk profile), the implementation (authority to proceed), and supporting product disclosure (PDS) used for that decision.
advice_event.identity: Derived from the advice record at its centre. Keyed on client + advice-record date + subject matter/scope.
advice_event.sequence_note: A client accumulates multiple advice events over time (e.g. super advice year 1, insurance year 2). Each is its own nested folder. Events are ordered by date but NOT assumed to be related unless documents link them.

special_folders.name: _Client-level documents
special_folders.holds: Documents tied to the client but not to any single advice event — chiefly the FSG, and general correspondence.
special_folders.why: Forcing these into an event folder would be wrong; they belong to the relationship, not one decision.

special_folders.name: _Needs review
special_folders.holds: Any document the tool cannot confidently place into a client and/or an advice event.
special_folders.why: Orphans and low-confidence items must surface, never be filed into a guessed location. This folder is the visible home of the flagging queue.

shared_document_rule.case: A document (e.g. a PDS) legitimately relates to more than one advice event.
shared_document_rule.default: File once, at the event where first used; reference from other events rather than duplicating.
shared_document_rule.note: Firms differ. Leave duplicate-vs-reference as a per-firm setting.

filing_model.accuracy_mechanism: Because a document is placed by two axes that must agree (correct client AND a coherent advice event), a document naming a client but referencing a non-existent event, or vice versa, is a disagreement that fires a flag. Single-axis filing would silently misplace it.
filing_model.human_in_the_loop: Event grouping is always a proposal a human confirms, never silent auto-bundling. Confidence is visible per document and per event. Mis-grouping is expected early because it depends on link accuracy — the fiddliest part of the system.
filing_model.build_note: Client-outer/event-inner is a nesting rule over results already produced. Keep the storage layer abstracted so the folder scheme (and later, local-folder vs cloud-bucket) can change without touching the classifier.

summary_feature.status: PLANNED — a later phase, after classification and filing are working and trusted.
summary_feature.purpose: Generate a plain-English summary per advice event (not per loose document), leveraging the fact that documents are already grouped into a coherent bundle.
summary_feature.why_event_level: Summarising a whole advice event ('here is the March 2024 super consolidation advice: the recommendation, the basis, what it cost, whether it was authorised') is far more useful than summarising one document in isolation.
summary_feature.inputs: The grouped documents of one advice event.
output_shape: cost to client and benefits to provider
whether inputs (fact find, risk profile) were present and consistent
any flags raised on the event

critical_cautions.not_advice: The summary describes documents that already exist. It must never generate, alter, or recommend advice — doing so would cross into providing financial advice and change the whole regulatory posture.
critical_cautions.human_verified: Summaries are drafts for a human to check against the source documents, not authoritative statements. Same human-in-the-loop principle as classification.
critical_cautions.hallucination_risk: An LLM summarising a document can invent facts not present. For a compliance-adjacent tool this is a serious failure mode; summaries must be checkable against, and traceable to, the source text.
critical_cautions.sequencing: Do not build this until classification and grouping are reliable. A summary built on mis-grouped documents is confidently wrong.

confidence_policy.purpose: The classifier reports its own confidence. That number is a claim by the model about itself, not a measurement, and nothing checked it before acting on it. This turns it into evidence that can be checked: every phrase the model says it matched is looked for in the document, and the scope gate's independent reading is compared against the type the model chose.
confidence_policy.direction_rule: Verification can only LOWER the acted-on confidence, never raise it. A model that quotes accurately has told the truth about its own reasoning; it has not thereby proved the answer right. Allowing evidence to inflate a number the model invented would launder a guess into a measurement.
confidence_policy.two_numbers: `confidence_raw` keeps the model's own figure unchanged, so drift in the model is visible over time and the two can be compared in the failure log. `confidence` is what the system acts on, and is what review_policy's thresholds are applied to.

signal_verification.rule: Each phrase in `matched_signals` must actually occur in the extracted text. The proportion that do becomes a multiplier.
signal_verification.matching: Case-insensitive, with ALL whitespace removed from both sides before comparing — not exact, and not merely whitespace-collapsed. PDF extraction splits words internally: the real ASIC samples produce 'A ustralian S ecurities' and 'h is advice', where the space sits inside the word, so collapsing runs of spaces does not help. Exact or collapsed matching would report honest quotes as fabricated on almost every real PDF, and a check that fires on everything gets ignored.
signal_verification.matching_trade_off: Removing whitespace makes matching looser, and a short signal can match inside an unrelated word ('ROA' sits inside 'BROADWAY'). Tolerable here in a way it is not in the scope gate, because this only decides whether to LOWER confidence: a loose match declines to penalise and never promotes anything. Wrongly calling an honest quote fabricated is the more damaging error, because it sends correct classifications of ordinary documents to review.
signal_verification.no_signals_why: A model naming a type while quoting nothing has given an answer with no working. That is not a fabrication, so it is not zero, but it is not evidence either. Halved rather than rejected, because the flag and the review threshold still get to see the proposal.

scope_agreement.rule: The scope gate reads the title region deterministically, by knowledge-base title patterns, with no model involved. Where it names a type and the classifier names a different one, two independent readings disagree.
scope_agreement.no_scope_type_why: The gate having no opinion is not disagreement. It only reads the first 500 characters, so a document whose title sits below that window leaves it silent — that is absence of evidence, and must not be scored as evidence of absence.
scope_agreement.why_it_is_worth_something: The gate is not smarter than the classifier, and on its own it is weak — it matches title strings. Its value is INDEPENDENCE: it cannot be wrong in the same way a language model is wrong, so agreement between them is worth more than either alone. This is the same argument filing_model.accuracy_mechanism makes about two axes having to agree.

confidence_policy.formula: confidence = confidence_raw x signal_factor x scope_factor, clamped to [0, 1]. Deliberately multiplicative and deliberately simple: a reviewer looking at a lowered number should be able to see which of the two checks lowered it, and by how much, without reading Python.
confidence_policy.calibration_status: The two factors are judgements, not fitted values — nothing has been measured against a scored sample set, because the classifier is not wired to one. They encode a direction (unverified quotes and cross-reading disagreement should both reduce trust) and a rough weight, not an observed error rate.

review_policy.purpose: Decides whether a classification is confident enough to act on, or must go to a human first. Ground rule #2: nothing files silently, and a document that cannot be placed confidently routes to _Needs review WITH A REASON rather than leaving the pipeline. The reason is the point — 'needs review' on its own tells a reviewer nothing about what to look at.
review_policy.threshold_meaning: The classifier's confidence must MEET OR EXCEED the type's threshold for the proposal to stand on its own. Below it, the document still gets its proposed type and its reasoning — it is not discarded — but it is marked needs_review with the low_confidence reason.
review_policy.calibration_status: These numbers are a first domain judgement, not a measurement. Nothing has been measured against a scored sample set yet, because the classifier is not wired to one. They are set by the COST OF BEING WRONG per document type, which is knowable now, rather than by observed accuracy, which is not. Expect to move them once the failure log has entries.
review_policy.why_per_type: A single global threshold treats every document as equally expensive to misplace, and they are not. Misfiling a PDS puts a product brochure in the wrong folder. Misfiling an SOA puts the advice record — the centre of the advice event, the thing every other document links to — under the wrong client or the wrong event.
review_policy.default_note: Applies to any document type without its own entry, so adding a type to `documents` needs no edit here (ground rule #1). A new type starts cautious and earns a lower bar once its behaviour is known.

soa.why: The advice record, and the centre of an advice event — version status, superseding, event grouping and every links_to relationship key on finding the right one. A wrong SOA is not one misfiled document; it is an advice event assembled around the wrong document.

roa.why: Also an advice record (advice_record_role is true), with the same event-grouping weight as an SOA. It carries the roa_basis_unconfirmed question regardless of confidence, so a low-confidence ROA is a document a reviewer is already being asked about — no reason to let a shaky type through underneath a question.

authority_to_proceed.why: A signed client authorisation, and the link between advice and what was actually implemented. atp_without_advice_record is one of the three high-severity flags in the set, so a misread ATP either fires it wrongly or hides a genuine gap.

fee_disclosure_statement.why: Fee disclosure and ongoing-fee consent carry their own compliance exposure, and fds_era_mismatch depends on this type being identified correctly before the pre/post-DBFO check can run at all.

fact_find.why: An input document evidencing safe harbour steps 1-2. Wrong placement is recoverable and visible — a fact find in the wrong folder is obvious to the next person who opens it — but fact_find_after_soa sequencing depends on it.

risk_profile.why: Input document, pairs with the fact find. risk_mismatch is high severity but compares CONTENT to an SOA's recommendations, so it needs the type read correctly first.

fsg.why: Licensee-wide and not client-specific: the same edition is given to every client, so a misfiled FSG misplaces a copy of a document the firm holds many identical copies of. Lowest cost of error in the set, and highly standardised titling, so a lower bar costs little.

pds.why: Issued by the product provider, not the firm, and not client-specific. Reference material rather than a record of anything the firm did. Same reasoning as the FSG.

reason_codes.unreadable: The file could not be opened at all — encrypted with a user password, corrupt, truncated, or not really a PDF. A property of the FILE, and the most specific answer available: nothing was read, so nothing else can be said about it. Distinct from a file that opened and held no text, and from one that was read in full and matched nothing. Before this existed the pipeline raised and returned HTTP 500, so a reviewer got a stack trace instead of a document.
reason_codes.no_selectable_text: The file opened but carries no extractable text — a scan or a photograph of a document. Nothing is wrong with it; it simply cannot be read without OCR (#5). It is NOT out of scope: a scanned Statement of Advice is still a Statement of Advice, and treating it as 'not advice' is what #22 was about.
reason_codes.out_of_scope: No document type matched at the scope gate. Previously a dead end — the document left the pipeline with no type, no confidence and no flag, indistinguishable from an unreadable file. It is now a review reason: something arrived and the tool could not place it, which is exactly what a human should see.
reason_codes.unknown_type: The classifier returned no type. Distinct from out_of_scope: the title gate DID match something, so the document looks like one of ours and the classifier still could not name it.
reason_codes.low_confidence: The classifier named a type but below that type's threshold. The proposal and its reasoning are still returned — a reviewer confirming a correct low-confidence answer is useful failure-log data.
reason_codes.classifier_unavailable: The classifier could not be reached at all. Not a property of the document, and must never be recorded as a classification failure against it.
reason_codes.flagged_blocking: A flag fired that blocks on its own. Usually high severity, but a rule may override its severity’s default — multi_doc_bundle is medium and blocks, because filing a two-document bundle as one document destroys a record rather than mislabelling one. Named for what it does rather than for its severity, because those came apart the moment overrides existed.

correction_reasons.purpose: Why a reviewer's answer differs from the tool's — or that it does not. The failure log's one-line why (ground rule #6) is built from one of these codes, never typed: a free-text box at the end of a review is exactly where a client name gets written by somebody being helpful. Adding a reason is a knowledge-base edit, not a code change.

codes.confirmed: The tool's type was right; the document was held for review anyway — low confidence, a blocking flag, or out of scope. Logged because thresholds are calibrated from confirmations as much as from corrections: a type a reviewer confirms nearly every time it is held is being held too often.
codes.lookalike: The document quotes, cites or resembles another type and was read as that one — an SOA that refers to a PDS, an ROA read as an SOA, an FSG section inside an SOA.
codes.non_standard_title: The document's own title is missing, firm-branded or worded differently from the title patterns, so the tool had no title to go on.
codes.poor_text: The text the tool read was incomplete or garbled — a scan, a partial extraction, a redacted or image-heavy page. A property of the file rather than of the rules.
codes.bundle: One file holds more than one document, and the tool named only one of them.
codes.knowledge_base_gap: None of the above: the knowledge base is missing a rule. The record says a gap exists; what the gap is belongs in an issue, not in the log.

review_policy.forces_review_decision: RESOLVED by multi_doc_bundle. Severity sets the default (edge_case_flags.severity_forces_review: only high blocks). A rule may override it with its own `forces_review`. Medium stays non-blocking by default because roa_basis_unconfirmed fires on every ROA and a queue that asks about every document gets ignored — see the direction note on #20. multi_doc_bundle is medium and overrides to blocking, because filing a two-document bundle as one document destroys a record rather than mislabelling one. It is the only override today.

approval_policy.purpose: Who may approve a filing proposal, what they check, and which flags block approval outright. Decided by Bella on 1 Oct 2026 for the Approve/Edit/Reject screen (build step 5, #4). Read by that screen; never restated in code (ground rule #1).
approval_policy.default_for_any_firm: A sensible default for an Australian advice practice. Firms differ — a small practice may have no paraplanner, or an adviser who is also compliance — and adjusting roles per firm waits for a real pilot (#26 rule).

paraplanner.who: Drafts advice and researches products under an adviser; does not sign advice.

adviser.who: Authorised representative / relevant provider. Gives and signs the advice and holds the best-interests duty for it.

compliance.who: Compliance officer acting for the licensee, which must monitor advice quality.

approval_policy.approvers_note: Only an adviser or a compliance officer approves. Everyone else can prepare and correct a proposal, which saves the adviser time without moving the decision.
approval_policy.own_clients_only_note: An adviser approves these only for their own clients: one adviser must not sign off another's advice record. Compliance may approve any.
approval_policy.reviewer_check: Read the title and skim the content to confirm the name and the filing are right.

checks_by_type.fsg: Right licensee and edition; dated before the advice was given.
checks_by_type.fact_find: Right client; dated before the SOA it underpins.
checks_by_type.risk_profile: Right client; the risk category is stated.
checks_by_type.file_note: Right client; a note ABOUT advice, never the advice itself.
checks_by_type.pds: The product is one recommended or considered in the advice.
checks_by_type.soa: Right client; the advice-as-at (commencement) date; the subject from its own scope.
checks_by_type.roa: As SOA, plus which of the three ROA situations applies.
checks_by_type.authority_to_proceed: Signed; links to the SOA or ROA it authorises.
checks_by_type.fee_disclosure_statement: Right client; the period; consent signed.

flag_effects.hard_stop: Approve is unavailable until the problem is fixed. Only compliance may clear it.
flag_effects.warning: Shown to the approver, who may still approve.

flag_effect_by_rule_why.atp_without_advice_record: Implementation with no advice on file is a serious compliance gap.
flag_effect_by_rule_why.risk_mismatch: Goes straight to whether the advice is appropriate.
flag_effect_by_rule_why.fact_find_after_soa: Suggests the advice was written before the client was understood.
flag_effect_by_rule_why.multi_doc_bundle: Filing a bundle as one document loses a record; stop until split.
flag_effect_by_rule_why.no_date: The approver can read the date and enter it.
flag_effect_by_rule_why.fds_era_mismatch: Often only an old template, but worth a look.
flag_effect_by_rule_why.roa_basis_unconfirmed: Asks which ROA situation applies; the approver answers it.

approval_policy.not_yet_decided_note: Rules Bella has not yet placed as hard stop or warning. Until she does, the screen treats them as warnings — and low_confidence and unknown_type already send the document to review.

proposed_warnings_not_yet_rules.fsg_edition_out_of_date: The FSG edition was not the one in force at the advice date. Needs edition dates per licensee.
proposed_warnings_not_yet_rules.pds_product_not_in_advice: The PDS's product is not named in the SOA or ROA. Needs cross-document state (#8).
proposed_warnings_not_yet_rules.file_note_names_provider: A file note naming a provider is easily mistaken for that provider's document.

edge_case_flags.purpose: Rules that route a document to the internal human-review queue instead of forcing a category. Each fires a flag; it does not silently reclassify.

evaluation_values.stateless: Everything the rule needs is inside the one document. Answerable at ingest, with no other file on record.
evaluation_values.stateful: Needs other documents for the same client — a prior SOA, an earlier fact find, a competing current version. Not answerable until documents persist across requests.

edge_case_flags.evaluation_note: Every rule declares which it is, so the flagging engine can never claim to have evaluated a rule whose evidence it does not hold. Declaring a rule stateless says it CAN be answered at ingest, not that it is implemented yet.
edge_case_flags.severity_note: Whether a flag on its own sends a document to _Needs review. A flag is always SHOWN; this decides whether it blocks. High severity means the document cannot be acted on until a person looks. Medium and low attach a question to a proposal that still stands on its own confidence — a rule can override its severity with `forces_review` — see review_policy.forces_review_decision.

rules.trigger: Any document classified as an ROA. Fires on every one, not on an anomaly.
rules.why: An ROA is permitted in three situations — further advice (reg 7.7.10AE), no buy or sell (reg 7.7.10AAA), small investment (s946AA) — and which one applies changes the content the record must contain and whether a prior SOA is required at all. The document type does not settle it, so filing an ROA without recording its basis loses the fact that determines what a compliant record looks like. This is a confirmation, never an error: all three are valid.
rules.asks: Which of the three situations is this? Where the text supports exactly one, the flag proposes it with the phrases it matched, so a reviewer confirms or corrects one thing rather than starting from scratch.

determination_values.proposed: Signals for exactly one basis. The flag names it and cites the matched phrases.
determination_values.ambiguous: Signals for more than one basis. The flag lists the candidates; it does not pick.
determination_values.absent: No basis signal found. The honest default — the flag asks which kind, and proposes nothing.

rules.not_to_be_confused_with: roa_without_soa asks a cross-document question (is there a prior SOA on file?) and needs state this rule does not. They can both fire on the same document and they are asking different things.

rules.trigger: Further-advice-style ROA identified but no prior SOA on file for the client
rules.why: A further-advice ROA (notional s946B(2)-(3) / reg 7.7.10AE) depends on an existing SOA. The other two situations — no buy or sell (reg 7.7.10AAA) and small investment (s946AA) — do not, so this is a 'confirm which kind', not an automatic error.

rules.trigger: Authority to Proceed with no matching SOA/ROA on file
rules.why: An authorisation to implement advice that isn't on file — either a bundle-split miss or a genuine gap.

rules.trigger: Fact Find dated later than the SOA it should underpin
rules.why: Advice may predate the information it was supposedly based on (best-interests concern).

rules.trigger: Risk Profile category not reflected in SOA recommendations
Single file appears to contain more than one document type (classic: SOA + appended Authority to Proceed)
rules.why: Needs splitting before records and links are accurate. Left unsplit, the appended document never becomes a record of its own — so atp_without_advice_record fires on correctly-executed advice, which is the fastest way to get a firm to ignore the review queue.
rules.forces_review_why: Overrides the severity default. Medium normally attaches a question without blocking, because a queue that asks about every document gets ignored. This rule is the override review_policy.forces_review_decision records: filing a two-document bundle as one document destroys a record rather than mislabelling one, and unlike a basis confirmation it cannot be corrected later from what was filed.
rules.asks: Does this file hold more than one document, and if so where does the second start?
rules.never_split_automatically: The flag proposes candidate boundaries as evidence; a human approves any split. A missed bundle is a flag nobody actioned. A WRONG split silently destroys a record by cutting a document in half, and nothing downstream can tell that it happened. Ground rule #2 applies with force.

pagination_restart.rule: A page-number marker reading 'page 1 of N' on any page other than the first. A document's own pagination restarting mid-file is direct evidence of a boundary, independent of titles, headers and type.
pagination_restart.pattern_note: The gap is tolerant because extraction pads it — the real RG 90 sample yields 'Page 2          of 23'.
pagination_restart.evidence: Validated on samples/soa_atp/asic-rg90-example-soa-with-atp.pdf, which is RG 90 itself followed by an example SOA whose footer restarts at 'Page 1 of 23' on page 31. Correctly silent on every single-document sample tested.

title_transition.rule: The document type implied by each page's leading region, read with the same title patterns the scope gate uses. A running header produces a CONSTANT type across pages; a boundary produces a CHANGE. So the signal is the transition, not the presence of a second type's name.
title_transition.why_not_frequency: Suppressing types that appear on most pages looks sensible and is wrong: in a real bundle the larger document's own running header legitimately appears on most pages of the whole file, so frequency-based suppression hides exactly the boundary being looked for.
title_transition.excursion_rule: A transition A -> B is ignored where A reappears after B, AND where B already appeared before it. Both halves are needed: the first ignores the departure into a section, the second ignores the file handing itself back to the type it already was. A section inside one document returns to its parent; an appended document does not. This is what separates a PDS with a 'risk profile' section from a PDS with something genuinely appended — without the second half, the RETURN from the excursion is reported as a boundary.
title_transition.known_weakness: A heading that names another document type, never returning to the parent, still reads as a boundary — a late 'Financial Services Guide' heading inside an SOA, for example. Candidates are evidence for a human, not a decision, so a wrong candidate costs a look rather than a record.
title_transition.evidence: Validated on two real ASIC documents that contain an appended Authority to Proceed as their final page: asic-cp284-example-soa-attachment.pdf (soa -> authority_to_proceed at p56) and asic-rg90-example-soa-2013.pdf (at p40). Also correctly suppressed a pds -> risk_profile -> pds excursion in unisuper-flexi-pension-pds.pdf.

detection.leading_region_note: The same window scope_gate.py reads, for the same reason: a document names other types in its body, and only the top of a page is its own heading.

rules.trigger: Document plays the advice-record role but titling is ambiguous between SOA and CAR
rules.why: During the DBFO transition both may appear; capture the correct statutory label. DORMANT: 'car' is not a document type while DBFO Tranche 2 is unlegislated, so nothing fires this today. Kept because the rule becomes live the moment the successor type is added back — see reform_watch.

rules.trigger: Fee/consent document format doesn't match the expected pre/post-DBFO-Tranche-1 era for its date
rules.why: Ongoing-fee consent mechanics changed under DBFO; wrong-era format may indicate a compliance gap.

rules.trigger: No date extractable from a document type that requires one for sequencing
rules.why: Version tracking and advice-timing checks impossible without a date.
Ambiguous or poor-quality document; needs a human eye.

rules.trigger: The classifier returned no document type at all. Distinct from low_confidence, where it named a type below that type's threshold.
rules.why: Possibly out-of-scope or a novel/edge document.

rules.trigger: Two candidate 'current' documents of the same type and scope for one client
rules.why: Cannot determine which is in force.
